title: Flutter by

clues.t: I taste with my feet.
I start life as an egg on a leaf.
Then I eat almost nonstop as a caterpillar.
I rebuild myself inside a chrysalis.
My wings are covered in tiny scales.
A flying insect with big colourful wings.

pearl: Monarch butterflies migrate up to 4,000 km, and no single butterfly makes the whole round trip.

title: Gum leaf diet

clues.t: I have fingerprints almost identical to a human’s.
My pouch opens towards my back legs.
I sleep up to 20 hours a day.
I eat almost nothing but eucalyptus leaves.
I’m not a bear, though people often call me one.
Grey, fluffy-eared Australian marsupial in a gum tree.

pearl: Eucalyptus is low in energy and toxic to most animals, which is why koalas sleep so much.

title: Tombs in the sand

clues.t: I’m the only Ancient Wonder of the World still standing.
My biggest member was the tallest human-made structure for about 3,800 years.
Workers, not slaves, built me, according to modern archaeologists.
A sphinx guards me.
I was built as tombs for pharaohs.
Three huge stone triangles outside Cairo.

pearl: The Great Pyramid was built around 2560 BCE for the pharaoh Khufu.

title: Clack clack ding

clues.t: Mark Twain was one of the first authors to hand in a book written on me.
My key layout was designed to stop bars jamming.
That layout still sits on your phone: QWERTY.
I ding when you reach the end of a line.
You need ink ribbon and paper to use me.
A machine for typing before computers.

pearl: Christopher Latham Sholes patented his typewriter in 1868; the QWERTY layout followed a few years later.

title: Spotted helper

clues.t: I’m a beetle, though my name says otherwise.
Farmers like me: I eat aphids.
One of me can eat thousands of aphids in my life.
When scared, I ooze a smelly yellow liquid from my knees.
Americans call me a bug.
Small round red beetle with black spots.

pearl: The ‘lady’ is thought to refer to the Virgin Mary, often painted in a red cloak.

title: Shadow clock

clues.t: I’m one of the oldest timekeeping tools.
I don’t work at night or on cloudy days.
My pointer is called a gnomon.
In Australia, my pointer has to point south.
I tell the time with a shadow.
A clock powered by the sun.

pearl: A sundial’s gnomon must point to the celestial pole: north in the northern hemisphere, south in the southern.

title: Ancient computer

clues.t: Sponge divers found me in a shipwreck in 1901.
I’m about 2,000 years old.
I was a lump of corroded bronze for decades before anyone understood me.
X-ray scans revealed at least 30 interlocking gear wheels.
I predicted eclipses and tracked the planets.
Often called the world’s first analogue computer, from a Greek island wreck.

pearl: Nothing with gearing this complex is known again until medieval astronomical clocks, over a thousand years later.

title: Lady of the skies

clues.t: I was born in Kansas in 1897.
I worked as a nurse’s aide in Canada during World War I.
In 1932 I became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic.
I helped found the Ninety-Nines, a group for women pilots.
In 1937 I vanished over the Pacific near Howland Island.
Famous American woman aviator who went missing on a round-the-world flight.

pearl: Her last flight left from Lae, in what is now Papua New Guinea. Today is International Women’s Day.

title: Bath time buddy

clues.t: Programmers explain their code to me to find bugs.
In 1992, thousands of my plastic cousins fell off a ship and floated the oceans for years.
Ernie from Sesame Street sang a song about me.
Most of me are made of plastic, not rubber.
I squeak when squeezed.
Small yellow bath toy that floats.

pearl: The 1992 spill helped oceanographers map currents as the toys washed up on beaches worldwide.

title: Which way?

clues.t: Chinese inventors used me first, made with lodestone.
Sailors relied on me before satellites.
I work because the Earth is a giant magnet.
My needle doesn’t point to true north, but magnetic north.
N, E, S and W are marked on me.
A navigation tool with a needle that points north.

pearl: Magnetic north wanders by tens of kilometres a year, so maps list the difference.

title: Can’t fly, won’t fly

clues.t: My nostrils are at the tip of my long beak.
My egg is huge: about a fifth of my body weight.
I come out mostly at night.
My wings are tiny and I can’t fly.
My name is also a nickname for my country’s people.
Brown, fluffy, flightless bird from New Zealand.

pearl: Kiwi have nostrils at the beak tip to sniff out worms underground, unique among birds.

title: Dots and dashes

clues.t: An American painter co-invented me in the 1830s.
The Titanic used me to call for help.
Sailors could send me with a flashing light.
My most famous message is three short, three long, three short.
Every letter is made of short and long signals.
Dots and dashes used for telegraph messages.

pearl: Samuel Morse was a successful portrait painter before he turned to the telegraph.

title: Red centre

clues.t: I’m about 550 million years old.
Most of my bulk is hidden underground.
I glow red at sunrise and sunset.
Climbing me was banned in 2019.
I’m sacred to the Aṉangu people.
Giant sandstone rock in the middle of Australia.

pearl: Uluru was handed back to its traditional owners in 1985 and is jointly managed with Parks Australia.

title: Never ending

clues.t: My digits never end and never repeat.
Archimedes squeezed me between two polygons.
People celebrate me on 14 March.
Computers have calculated me to over 100 trillion digits.
I start 3.14159.
The ratio of a circle’s circumference to its diameter.

pearl: Albert Einstein was born on 14 March 1879, which makes Pi Day a double celebration for some.

title: Beware the Ides

clues.t: I was kidnapped by pirates as a young man and promised to crucify them. I did.
The month of July is named after me.
I crossed the Rubicon river with my army.
I fixed the calendar: we still use a version of my leap year.
I was stabbed in the Senate on 15 March 44 BCE.
Roman general and dictator; ‘Et tu, Brute?’

pearl: Ancient writers say he was stabbed 23 times. Today is the Ides of March.

title: Seeds on the outside

clues.t: I’m not a true berry, botanically speaking.
I wear my seeds on the outside, about 200 of them.
Wimbledon serves me with cream.
I belong to the rose family.
I’m often dipped in chocolate.
Red, heart-shaped fruit with green leaves on top.

pearl: A banana is a true berry; a strawberry isn’t. Botany is strange.

title: Green for a day

clues.t: Halloween traces its roots to my ancient festival of Samhain.
Bram Stoker, who wrote Dracula, came from me.
My national symbol is a harp.
I’m nicknamed the Emerald Isle.
Rivers are dyed green around the world for my patron saint.
Island country whose capital is Dublin.

pearl: St Patrick’s Day is 17 March. St Patrick wasn’t Irish: he was born in Roman Britain.

title: Small bent wire

clues.t: Norwegians wore me as a protest symbol in World War II.
My most common design is called the Gem.
A man once traded one red one of me up to a house.
Microsoft once made me a cartoon helper called Clippy.
I’m usually made of bent steel wire.
Holds sheets of paper together.

pearl: Kyle MacDonald traded a red paperclip for bigger things, 14 trades later ending with a house.

title: The coathanger

clues.t: I opened on 19 March 1932.
At my opening, a man on horseback cut the ribbon before the Premier could.
My steel arch expands up to 18 cm on hot days.
I’m painted grey, and the job never really ends.
Tourists climb over my arch.
Big steel arch bridge next to the Opera House.

pearl: Francis de Groot of the New Guard slashed the ribbon with his sword. Happy birthday, bridge.

title: Equal day and night

clues.t: I happen twice a year.
On me, the Sun rises almost exactly due east.
My name comes from Latin for ‘equal night’.
In Australia, my March visit starts astronomical autumn.
The Sun sits right above the equator on me.
The day when day and night are about the same length.

pearl: Day and night aren’t exactly equal at the equinox, because the atmosphere bends sunlight over the horizon.

title: Five, seven, five

clues.t: I come from Japan.
Matsuo Bashō is my most famous master.
His frog jumping into an old pond is my best-known example.
I traditionally include a word for the season.
I have just three lines.
Short poem with 5, 7 and 5 syllables.

pearl: Today is World Poetry Day. In Japanese, haiku count sound units, not exactly syllables.

title: Life’s essential

clues.t: About 60% of your body is me.
I’m densest at 4 °C, which stops lakes freezing solid.
Ice floats because I expand when I freeze.
I cover about 71% of the Earth.
I can be solid, liquid or gas at everyday temperatures.
H₂O.

pearl: Today is World Water Day. Only about 3% of Earth’s water is fresh, and most of that is ice.

title: Bunch of them

clues.t: Botanically, I’m a berry.
I’m slightly radioactive, thanks to potassium.
My plant is technically a giant herb, not a tree.
Most of me sold worldwide are one variety, the Cavendish.
I come in bunches called hands.
Long yellow fruit you peel.

pearl: Cyclone Larry in 2006 wiped out most of Australia’s crop and prices jumped to about $12 a kilo.

title: Cube poo

clues.t: My pouch faces backwards so dirt doesn’t get in while I dig.
I can run at up to 40 km/h.
My bum is a tough plate of cartilage that I use to block my burrow.
My poo is cube-shaped.
I’m a burrowing Australian marsupial.
Stocky, short-legged marsupial that digs.

pearl: Wombat cubes form in the last part of the intestine, where the wall has stiffer and stretchier bands.

title: Square pockets

clues.t: I have my own international day on 25 March.
I’m cooked between two hot metal plates.
Nike’s first running shoe soles were made in one of my irons.
Belgium is famous for me.
My grid of square pockets holds syrup.
Crisp batter cake with a grid pattern.

pearl: Bill Bowerman poured rubber into his wife’s waffle iron to make a grippier sole.

title: Tiny worlds

clues.t: A Dutch cloth merchant made me famous in the 1670s.
He was first to see bacteria, calling them ‘little animals’.
Robert Hooke used me to name the cell.
My electron version can see individual atoms.
I use lenses to magnify.
Scientific instrument for seeing things too small for the eye.

pearl: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek made over 500 single-lens microscopes, some magnifying about 270 times.

title: Wooden O

clues.t: I was built in London in 1599.
Part of me was made from the timber of an older theatre.
A cannon fired during a play in 1613 set my thatched roof on fire.
Poorer audience members stood in my yard as ‘groundlings’.
A reconstruction of me opened in 1997.
Shakespeare’s theatre.

pearl: Today is World Theatre Day. The 1613 fire happened during Henry VIII; nobody died.

title: Sweet cross

clues.t: An old nursery rhyme says I cost one a penny or two a penny.
Superstition said I would never go mouldy if baked on Good Friday.
Sailors took me to sea to prevent shipwreck.
Some versions of me now come with chocolate chips.
I’m spiced and full of fruit.
Sweet bun marked with a cross, eaten at Easter.

pearl: Queen Elizabeth I once restricted their sale to funerals, Good Friday and Christmas. Happy Easter.

title: Our Easter animal

clues.t: My ears are long, like a rabbit’s.
My pouch faces backwards.
I never need to drink water: I get it from my food.
I’m endangered, partly because of foxes and cats.
Australians push me as a chocolate alternative to the Easter Bunny.
Small desert marsupial with big ears and a long snout.

pearl: Rabbits are a feral pest in Australia, so the Easter Bilby was promoted from the 1990s to raise conservation funds.

title: Rub it out

clues.t: I contain no lead at all.
My core is graphite mixed with clay.
On 30 March 1858, a patent was granted for my version with an eraser on top.
Most of me are painted yellow in the US.
I can draw a line about 56 km long.
Wooden writing stick you sharpen.

pearl: Yellow pencils signalled Chinese graphite, which was prized; the colour stuck.

title: Comes back

clues.t: The oldest known version of me, made from mammoth tusk, was found in Poland.
Most of my Aboriginal versions were made for hunting and don’t come back.
I was also used as a digging tool and to make fire.
My returning version spins and flies in a curve.
Astronauts tested me on the International Space Station.
Curved throwing stick from Australia that comes back.

pearl: Returning boomerangs work because spinning wings make uneven lift, which tips the flight path into a circle.
